name: Gareth Garcia

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for doing this, Gareth. I work for the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or government. Everything is confidential, so you can tell me your public line and also what you really think. What does a normal working day look like for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm a junior operator at Ridgeway Estates, which is two thousand acres of wheat and oilseed rape plus a beef yard with about four hundred steers. It's owned by an investment company, so the bosses are people in suits I've met twice. My day might be riding a GPS tractor, flying the spray drone over the rape, or mucking out and checking water in the beef yard. I've been there eighteen months, and I'm still the one who gets the jobs nobody else wants.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like most, and what grinds you down?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I love the drone, honestly, seeing a field from above and spotting the wet patch before it rots the crop. What grinds me down is that I'm still on the bottom rate and the beef yard work is cold and heavy. I share a house in the village with two lads from the feed merchant, and I've got about five months of rent and bills saved. No partner right now, which keeps things simple.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Every day. I photograph leaf spots and ask the AI what disease it is, I use it to plan the drone flight paths, and it writes my weekly logs for the farm manager. Half the older lads think I'm cheating. I think I'm just not wasting time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say AI turned out to be a good tool and nothing more, and that's fine. Online I'd probably post that the hype was about investors, not farmers. At work I'd tell the older lads they can stop worrying.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it means my plan still works: get good at the drones and the GPS kit and move up to operator rate. The only thing that stalls me is Ridgeway's pay scale, which moves slowly. My job feels secure, because they need someone young who doesn't mind the beef yard.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep using AI for my logs and disease checks, and ask the farm manager, Deborah, to send me on the advanced drone licence. I'd keep putting about a hundred and fifty a month into savings. Nothing dramatic.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels calm, a bit flat maybe. I like change, so a world where nothing moves is slightly boring.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the bosses are people in suits. Does that matter in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It matters in every picture. When something saves time at Ridgeway, the savings go up to the investment company, not down to us. I'd still want a share of what we save, even if AI only saves a bit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the advanced drone licence change for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: With the advanced drone licence I could fly bigger spray drones and over longer distances, and that's another two an hour on my rate at Ridgeway. More than that, it means Deborah sees me as the tech person, not just the beef yard kid.

say: AI turned out to be a **good tool**, nothing more, and that's **fine**.
The hype was about **investors**, not farmers.
think: My plan to move up to **operator rate** still works.
**Ridgeway's pay scale** moves slowly, which is the only drag.
They need someone young for the **beef yard**, so I'm secure.
do: Keep using AI for **weekly logs** and disease checks.
Ask Deborah for the **advanced drone licence**.
Save about **a hundred and fifty** a month.
feel: **Calm**, and a little **bored** by a world that doesn't move.
S0.quote: When something saves time at Ridgeway, the savings go up to the investment company, not down to us.
fieldNote: He's at ease with AI and sees **no threat** if it plateaus.
His political edge shows in **who gets the savings**, even from small gains.
The **drone licence** is as much about status as pay.

steps.text: Keep using AI for weekly logs and leaf-disease checks
Ask Deborah to fund the advanced drone licence
Save a hundred and fifty a month from the operator wage

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the moment for farm workers to get trained up, and the companies should pay for it. Online I'd post about workers needing a share of the gains. At work I'd offer to show the older lads the AI tools, because I'd rather they learn than get pushed out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it's good for me. The thinking tasks, like planning sprays, ordering seed and doing logs, go to software, and I'm already the one who uses it. Robots come slowly to the beef yard, and when they do, someone has to set them up and fix them. I'd want that someone to be me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd sign up for a farm robotics course at the agricultural college, probably the one-year evening certificate. I'd push Deborah to make me the go-to person for new kit, with a pay bump. And I'd try to get the lads at Ridgeway to join the landworkers' union, so if jobs shrink, we're not each on our own.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels exciting, mostly. The only bit that stings is watching older people get left behind.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at Ridgeway would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Colin, mainly. He's sixty, does the grain store and keeps the records in a paper book. The AI could do his ordering and stock records tomorrow, and he'd hate every minute of learning it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You want robots, but you worry about Colin. Is that a contradiction?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe a bit. I want the farm machines, I just don't want them owned by people who've never stood in the beef yard. If the workers got a share of what the robots save, I wouldn't feel bad about any of it.

say: This is the moment for farm workers to get **trained up**, paid by the **companies**.
Workers need a **share of the gains**, and I'd post that.
think: It's **good for me**, because I already use the software.
Someone has to **set up and fix** the robots, and I want that.
**Colin's records** and ordering are what software takes first.
do: Sign up for the **farm robotics** evening certificate.
Push Deborah to make me the **go-to person** for new kit, with a pay bump.
Get the Ridgeway lads to join the **landworkers' union**.
feel: Mostly **excited**, with a sting about older people **left behind**.
S1.quote: I want the farm machines, I just don't want them owned by people who've never stood in the beef yard.
fieldNote: He reads Steady Disruption as an **opportunity**, since the thinking tasks move to tools he already uses.
His worry is for **Colin**, not himself.
He admits a **contradiction**: pro-robot, but against who owns them.

steps.text: Enrol in the one-year farm robotics evening certificate
Become Ridgeway's go-to person for new AI kit
Recruit Ridgeway workers into the landworkers' union

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's too fast for anyone to handle fairly, and the government needs to step in with a basic income and public ownership of some of this tech. I'd post a lot. At work I'd tell the lads to get organised now, not in 2031.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it's scarier than I'd admit. The thinking AI in 2028 takes my best bits, the spray plans, the disease checks, the logs. Then around 2031 the robots arrive, and a robot can drive a tractor and fly a drone better than me. Maybe I fix them for a while, but the robot makers will send their own techs, or their own robots.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the two years before the robots, I'd move fast. I'd finish the robotics course in one year instead of two, and apply for field technician jobs with the robot companies, even if it means moving to another region. I'd push my savings up to two hundred a month. And I'd join any campaign for a robot dividend for workers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels like running for a train that's already moving. I'm excited and anxious in the same breath.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the robot makers might send their own techs. So is fixing robots really safe?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not forever, no. I think it buys me five or six years, maybe. After that I don't know, and I don't like not knowing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you really move region for a technician job?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, in a heartbeat. I've got no kids, no mortgage, just a shared house and a car. If a robot company in the north wants a farm tech who's actually mucked out a beef yard, I'd go.

say: It's **too fast** to handle fairly; we need a **basic income**.
Workers should get **organised now**, not in 2031.
think: In **2028** the AI takes my best bits: spray plans and disease checks.
Around **2031** robots drive tractors and fly drones better than me.
Fixing robots buys me maybe **five or six years**.
do: Finish the **robotics course** in one year, not two.
Apply for **field technician** jobs with robot makers, even in another region.
Raise savings to **two hundred** a month.
feel: Like **running for a train** that's already moving.
**Excited and anxious** at the same time.
S2.quote: If a robot company in the north wants a farm tech who's actually mucked out a beef yard, I'd go.
fieldNote: He's the first to say AGI takes his **thinking tasks** too, not just the hands-on ones.
He sees robot maintenance as a **temporary** shelter, not a safe harbour.
With no ties, **moving region** is easy for him.
His public line is **political**; privately he's more scared.

steps.text: Finish the farm robotics certificate in one year
Apply for field technician jobs with farm robot makers
Move to another region for a robot technician post
Save two hundred a month for the move

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough to make this fair if we start now, with worker-owned robots and training. I'd write that online. At Ridgeway I'd push for a plan where staff run the robots rather than get replaced by them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it feels workable. The thinking AI comes in 2031, so I've got four years to become the robotics person. The robots come around 2034. By 2034 I'd want to be running a robot fleet at Ridgeway, not driving a tractor. I'd be thirty-five, which is still young.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the robotics certificate over two years at a normal pace. I'd ask Deborah to let me trial a field robot on one block, with me in charge of it. And I'd keep saving, about a hundred and fifty a month, for a deposit on a used spray drone of my own.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels mostly good, with a nagging thought about where it ends.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why your own spray drone?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Small farms around here can't afford one, and I could spray for them on weekends. It's extra money and it's mine, not Ridgeway's. In five years I could have two drones and a van.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said it ends somewhere. Where?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Where nobody needs me at all, probably. I try not to think about that bit. Five years gives me time to be useful before that, and maybe the politics catches up.

Staff at Ridgeway should **run the robots**, not be replaced.

By **2034** I want to run a robot fleet, not drive a tractor.
At thirty-five I'd still be **young** enough to adjust.
do: Finish the **robotics certificate** over two years.
Ask Deborah to trial a **field robot** on one block, run by me.
Save for a **used spray drone** of my own.
feel: Mostly **good**, with a **nagging thought** about the end point.
S3.quote: By 2034 I'd want to be running a robot fleet at Ridgeway, not driving a tractor.
fieldNote: Five years lets him plan to **lead the change** at Ridgeway.
He's planning a **drone side business** for small farms.

steps.text: Finish the farm robotics certificate over two years
Run a trial field robot on one Ridgeway block
Save for a used spray drone to spray small farms

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is the right amount of time to do it well, so there's no excuse for doing it badly. I'd push the idea of farm robot co-ops, where small farms and workers share the machines. I'd post about that a lot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think this is the best picture for me. The thinking AI in 2036 and robots around 2039 give me twelve years. I could build a drone and robot contracting business and be the one who owns the kit. I'd be thirty-nine when the robots are everywhere, with my own business.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd buy a used spray drone this year and start spraying for small farms on weekends. I'd finish the robotics certificate at my own pace. And I'd talk to three or four small farmers about a co-op that buys a field robot together, with me running it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels great, honestly. Like I've been handed a map.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How much would the drone cost you, and where's the money from?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A used one is about six thousand. I'd put in two thousand from savings and borrow the rest from the machinery co-op's loan scheme. It'd pay back in two seasons if I get ten farms.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does owning the kit fit with what you said about who owns robots?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It does, if it's a co-op. I'm not against owning things, I'm against a fund in the city owning everything. If farmers and workers own the robots together, the money stays in the valley.

say: **Ten years** is the right time to do it well.
Small farms and workers should share machines through **robot co-ops**.
think: This is the **best picture** for me, with twelve years until robots.
I could own a **contracting business** by thirty-nine.
I'd be the one who **owns the kit**, not just runs it.
do: Buy a **used spray drone** for about six thousand this year.
Set up a **co-op** with three or four farmers to share a field robot.
S4.quote: If farmers and workers own the robots together, the money stays in the valley.
fieldNote: Ten years turns him from worker into **would-be owner**.
He squares his politics with business through a **co-op** model.
He has a costed plan: **six thousand**, with two from savings.

steps.text: Buy a used spray drone for about six thousand
Spray small farms in the valley on weekends
Form a co-op with nearby farmers to share a field robot
Finish the farm robotics certificate at my own pace

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because even the robot jobs I'm aiming at wouldn't last. What would help is a share of the gains for workers, like a robot dividend, and cheap loans so small farms and co-ops can own machines instead of just the big funds. And paid training while you work, not after you've been sacked.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask who owns the land. Everyone talks about robots, but whoever owns the land gets the robot money. That's the bit nobody puts in the adverts.

headlineQuote: Everyone talks about robots, but whoever owns the land gets the robot money.
portrait: Gareth is a **27-year-old** junior operator at Ridgeway Estates, a big farm owned by an **investment company**.
He uses AI **every day** and loves flying the spray drone.
He's pro-technology but angry about **who owns** the machines and the land.
With time, he plans to own drones and run a **robot co-op**; only AGI by 2028 makes him anxious.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because even robot technician jobs wouldn't **last**.
whatWouldHelp: A **robot dividend** for workers and **cheap loans** for co-ops.
